ev.q: The rate for occupational injury deaths for all workers decreased 45%, from 7.4 per 100,000 workers in 1980 to 4.1 in 1997.
Industries with the highest death rates were mining (30 per 100,000 workers), agriculture/forestry/fishing (19), and construction (15).
Since 1980, motor-vehicle crashes accounted for 24% of deaths and were the leading cause of injury-related death for U.S. workers.
During 1980--1997, 103,945 civilian workers died in the United States from occupational injuries, an average of 16 work-related deaths per day.
Males accounted for 93% of all deaths, with a death rate approximately 11 times that of females ( Table 1 ).

equity.level_reason: Death rates are reported by race (Black 5.6 vs White 5.0 per 100,000) and described, but values are only set side by side with no computed contrast or disparity framing. The sex ratio (11 times) and age rates lack social-position framing; industry and occupation are exposure routes, not SES.

level_alternative.reason: Race appears only once in the text and in Table 1 as a descriptive breakdown; a stricter reader could treat it as a descriptor rather than described group-specific results.

ev.q: Although 85% of civilian workers who died were white, blacks had a higher fatality rate (5.6 per 100,000 workers) than whites (5.0).
Males accounted for 93% of all deaths, with a death rate approximately 11 times that of females ( Table 1 ).
workers aged > 65 years had the highest age-specific death rate ( Table 1 ).
do not reflect the difference in exposure for groups that commonly work <40 hours per week (e.g., youth and older workers).

equity.equity_measurement: Race has only White, Black and Other categories (no ethnicity); denominators are CPS employment counts, not hours worked; rates are not calculated for unknown race.

notes: All rates are crude rates computed by hand from death counts and CPS employment denominators; no tests or CIs. The Healthy People 2010 target (3.2 per 100,000) is cited but not explicitly compared. CFOI counts are cited from another report for comparison, not analyzed.
view_issues: Table 1 is an OCR image; the '>=65' age row is OCR'd as '265'. The text's 'aged > 65' likely means ≥65. The Table 1 rates are for the whole 1980–1997 period, while the text also cites 1980 and 1997 rates not shown in a table.
